newsitem.title: USA: Dlr bulls go slow, but see no G7 "stop" sign yet.
newsitem.headline: Dlr bulls go slow, but see no G7 "stop" sign yet.

text.p: Dollar bulls tapped the brakes after the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations said they would monitor exchange rates and cooperate as appropriate, but dealers said they do not expect a red light much before 130 yen or 1.75 marks.

"Those will be the test levels that will give the G7 guys an opportunity to put their money where their mouth is," said Frank Pusateri, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Boston. "Right now there is definitely a buy-on-dips mentality on the street."

Unsurprisingly, in their statement on Sunday, policy makers from Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada and the United States refreshed old warnings against excessive exchange rate volatility and said currency values should reflect economic fundamentals.

The fairly tame document, issued after a five-hour meeting in Washington, did little to scare off long-term dollar buyers. The statement seemed designed to sap velocity from the dollar's rally rather than express displeasure over the dollar's present levels, analysts said.
"I wouldn't even say its a yellow light here in terms of dollar buying, maybe it's a 'go-slow' sign," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"I'm not sure its an invitation, but certainly I think the market is going to test that pain threshold," Gilmore added.

After the communique was announced, the dollar hoofed it to 1.7395 marks, a marginal new high for the year and its best level since February 1994. But the rallied fizzled, as caution reasserted itself and profit-taking kicked in.

For dollar/yen, however, the wording seemed to have a bit more of a bite than the G7 statement issued in February in Berlin. The dollar popped above 127 yen in early trade on Monday but yielded to selling and was unable to retest its 1997 high near 127.20.
The message from Berlin was essentially that exchange rates had corrected the major misalignments seen in early 1995, when the dollar was sitting near record lows.

The twist on Sunday was the emphasis on avoiding exchange rates that could lead to the reemergence of large external imbalances -- taken as a poorly-veiled reference to the weak yen and Japan's growing trade surplus.
The G7's attention, therefore, is likely to be lopsided towards dollar/yen, if and when they chose to make a stand against further dollar appreciation, dealers said.

"If we get near 130 on yen, there will be some intervention," Pusateri predicted. "If dollar/mark happens to be also 1.75, maybe they'll intervene in the marks too. If it's not, they'll just do yen. The yen will be the catalyst."
The policy makers were telling the markets to stay-tuned, analysts said.

If the bilateral trade balance between Japan and the United States starts to widen significantly, then G7 officials will have difficulty justifying dollar/yen's current high levels, based on the economic fundamentals, they said.
But at this point, as Richard Vullo, a vice president at Bayerische Hypotheken and Weschelsbank concluded: "Nobody really thinks you'll see anything like intervention until close to 130 yen."
At 1400 EDT/1800 GMT on Monday, the dollar was trading at 1.7305/10 marks, compared to 1.7270/80 at Friday's close and at 126.77/87 yen, up from 126.20/30.
